sources.headline: Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack
sources.text: Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement.It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes.Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man.Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.In the aftermath of the strikes, Syria said it had closed the ⁠Nassib border crossing with Jordan, suspending ⁠traffic in both directions. Nassib is Jordan’s only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.Earlier on Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said.The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown.Later on Monday, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman.The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri”, a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group.“They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men.Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”.“If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters.Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday.Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief.“Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief, and the grief of the Jordanian people – not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka.“Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station.But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.”

sources.headline: Jordan launches air strikes in Syria in response to a fatal church shooting
sources.text: DEVELOPING STORY, Syria denies prior coordination with Jordan after deadly air strikes hit two provinces, killing at least seven people.Jordan has carried out air strikes in Syria in retaliation for last week’s deadly church attack, with Syrian authorities saying the raids killed at least seven people, including three children and a woman.The attacks on Monday prompted Syria to close its main crossing with Jordan.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syrialist 2 of 3Jordan arrests three suspects over church attack in dawn raid: What to knowlist 3 of 3Jordan arrests three suspects over deadly church attackend of listJordan’s Armed Forces said in a statement that it targeted “hideouts” of armed groups in southeastern Syria in “retaliation” for the gun attack at a church in its Karak governorate on Friday. At least nine people were killed and dozens more wounded in those attacks.The Jordanian military said its retaliatory strikes were launched “in coordination with the Syrian government”.It said the strikes “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”.Syria, however, has denied coordinating with the Jordanian military.The Syrian government said in a statement that it has launched an investigation.Syria’s civil defense service said at least four sites in rural Daraa and Sweida Provinces were hit on Monday evening, and that its crews had recovered the bodies of seven people: three men, a woman and three children.Five of the dead — a man, a woman and three children — were members of one family killed in a strike on a tent in the village of Al Tai in Daraa Province, the service said. Three other family members, including a child, were wounded.A second strike hit Al Shayyah, also in Daraa, killing an 80-year-old man. A third hit a residential building in Muzayrib, in the Ain al-Basal area of Daraa, causing no casualties.A fourth struck a residential building in the town of Shahba in Sweida Province, killing a 60-year-old man.After the strikes, Syria’s border authority closed the Nassib crossing, suspending traffic in both directions. Nassib is the only crossing for passengers and commercial goods between Jordan and Syria.Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law on suspicion of involvement in the church attack. The arrested took place in the village of Al-Jadeeda, after a shootout with authorities.A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the suspects sustained serious injuries during the confrontation, which lasted for about three hours.The arrests and air strikes in Syria come after Jordan’s King Abdullah II pledged a stern response to the church attack. During the attack, three gunmen opened fire on mourners at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 56 miles south of the capital, Amman.The king said those responsible would face the “harshest penalties” and ordered a review of the country’s security procedures.Karak is home to a minority Christian population, which makes up about 300,000 of Jordan’s 11.5 million people.

Jordan's strikes on Syria over church terror attack kill several civilians

Jordanian authorities on Monday arrested three suspects over last week's terror attack that killed nine people in a church funeral procession in the village of Hammoud. Jordan's military later launched strikes on "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria in retaliation for the attack by alleged Islamic extremists, killing at least eight civilians including women and children, a health official said. 

Issued on: 26/10/2026 - 16:12
Modified: 26/10/2026 - 22:37

3 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
A funeral was held for people killed in an attack on a church in Hammoud, Karak region, southern Jordan, on October 25, 2026. © Ahmad Shoura, AFP

Jordan said it had struck "terrorist organisations" in neighbouring Syria on Monday in retaliation for an attack on a Christian church last week that killed nine people – just hours after confirming they had arrested the three assailants responsible, wounding them in a dawn raid and shootout.

Jordan's Public Security Directorate said the assailant group were cornered at an abandoned house where they had barricaded themselves inside and opened fire on security forces. 

"All three terrorists have been injured. They have been taken to hospital and are still receiving treatment," Director of Public Security Major General Abdullah Al-Maaytah told a press conference. 

Later Monday, the Jordanian military announced retaliatory strikes in southern Syria, saying air force jets had "destroyed several terrorist positions" and killed and wounded "numerous members" of groups linked to the perpetrators of the attack.

Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes on the southern Syrian province of Daraa. The director of health for the region told Syria's state-run SANA news agency that at least eight civilians had been killed, including women, children and a 65-year-old man.

READ MORE
Several killed, dozens wounded in Jordan church shooting

On Friday, the gunmen stormed the compound of the Greek Orthodox St George's Church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate during a funeral procession, authorities said. 

Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population. 

The arrested suspects – two brothers and another man related by marriage – are Islamic extremists, Maaytah said, adding they will be investigated and brought before the courts. 

 "This country must remain an oasis of security and stability, and we affirm that Jordan will remain impervious to anyone who dares to challenge it," he said. 

One of the suspects was in critical condition, Jordan's state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka reported. There were no casualties among security forces, it added. 

Under Jordanian law, murder is punishable by death by hanging. 

Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare. In 2016 an attack in Karak targeted a security centre and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead. 

A number of weapons and a large quantity of ammunition were seized from the three suspects, the Public Security Directorate said.  

'We will show them' 

Jordan's King Abdullah II said in a post on X that security forces "chased them to the very end".  

Before news of the strikes on Syria, he wrote, "We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated."  

"We will show them," he added. 

Earlier, the king visited wounded victims of the church attack in hospital, dressed in military fatigues and carrying a pistol on his hip.  

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al-Mamlaka on Monday that the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack". 

"There is no indication of any external contacts or collaboration with foreign parties," he said. 

Government communications minister Mohammad al-Momani said in response to the church attack "we stand ready and will strike with an iron fist, without mercy or leniency, against anyone who attempts to undermine Jordan's security".  

On Friday, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning for the victims of the church attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions. 

Eight of the nine victims were laid to rest on Sunday next to the church in a funeral that drew a huge crowd amid a large security presence, AFP images showed. 

The ninth person, Mohammed al-Qasous, was buried in south Amman on Monday. 

(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)

sources.headline: Three men arrested in shootout after deadly attack on church in Jordan
Jordan says 3 arrested in deadly attack on Greek Orthodox church
sources.text:
October 26, 2026 / 3:10 AM EDT
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
Amman, Jordan — Jordanian security forces arrested three men Monday for an attack on a Greek Orthodox church that killed nine people and wounded more than two dozen.The Public Security Directorate said the three suspects were arrested following a dawn shootout and that all three were wounded. No members of the security forces were injured in the dawn operation in Karak governorate, south of Jordan's capital, Amman. Karak is home to a minority Christian population. The attack on the Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak took place Friday during a funeral. Three men were reported to have taken part in the attack.
Some 3,000 people attended a funeral on Oct. 25, 2026 for victims of a terrorist attack two days earlier at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud, Jordan.
Salah Malkawi / Getty Images
There was still no claim of responsibility, and no armed group has been accused of the attack. Jordan's Interior Minister, Mazen Al-Faraya, identified the three men as those responsible for the attack. "The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," he said in a phone interview with state TV Al-Mamlaka. "They put up fierce resistance against the security forces, but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."
A bloodstain is seen in Saint George's Greek Orthodox Church, where gunmen opened fire during a funeral on Oct. 23, 2026 in the village of Hammoud, in Karak governorate in Jordan.
Alaa Al Sukhni / REUTERS
He added that there "are three individuals involved; they were identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident, and the security services employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
The directorate said, "Terrorism has no place among us," and that the three had met their "just fate," according to the Reuters news agency. The directorate didn't name the suspects or point to any possible links to any Islamist militant groups, Reuters added.King Abdullah II directed authorities to respond with "an iron fist" against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

sources.headline: Jordan says its air force struck ‘militant hideouts’ in Syria after church attack
sources.text: AL-JUDAYYDA, Jordan/CAIRO – Jordan said on Oct 26 its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week’s deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to “terrorist groups” operating there.The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus. Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.Damascus informed Jordan of its “complete reservation” over the strikes without prior coordination, the foreign ministry said in a statement.Seven people, including three children and a woman, were killed and three others were wounded in the Jordanian strikes, the Syrian Civil Defence said in a preliminary report.It said emergency teams responded to four sites hit by the strikes in the countryside of Daraa and Sweida provinces.There was no immediate comment from Jordan on that account.Shortly after the strikes, Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Oct 27, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, citing developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement.Nassib is Jordan’s only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.Earlier on Oct 26, senior government security officials said their security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Oct 26 over the church violence that killed nine people.“God willing, they only represent themselves,” said Jordan’s Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah.Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. The Oct 23 attack on the Christian minority prompted King Abdullah to order security forces to respond with an “iron fist”.In a press conference, al-Maaytah and Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism.“The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells,” al-Faraya added.Attack targeted Greek orthodox funeralThe Oct 23 assault during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, about 120km south-west of the capital, Amman, also wounded at least 34 people. Witnesses said gunmen opened fire for several minutes.The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials. The three suspects were named in the press briefing.Reuters video footage showed a building pockmarked by the exchange of fire in the village of al-Judayyda, in Karak governorate.Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said in a statement carried by state media that security forces located the suspects while they were hiding in an abandoned house. They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them.No security personnel were injured, and security forces found a number of firearms and rounds of ammunition in the suspects’ possession.There has been no claim of responsibility for the church attack.Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, has foiled Islamist militant plots in the past. The security officials did not name any Islamist groups in the press conference. REUTERS

sources.headline: Gunmen open fire at a church during a funeral in Jordan, killing 7 and wounding 40
sources.text:
A man looks through a gap in a stone wall toward a Greek Orthodox church where gunmen opened fire during a funeral hours earlier in Hamoud village, in Jordan's Karak governorate on Friday.
AP Photo/AP
hide caption
AP Photo/AP
JERUSALEM — Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said. The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 90 kilometers (55 miles) south of the capital, Amman. Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church. Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.
Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. "It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire," Halasa said. He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan's security services did not immediately release details. A government statement said that the attack was "carried out by unknown assailants," but didn't say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that "investigations are underway at full speed." Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom's Petra News Agency.
Soldiers and security officers hold back residents outside Prince Ali Military Hospital during King Abdullah II's visit to people wounded when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church hours earlier, in Karak, Jordan on Friday.
AP Photo/AP
hide caption
AP Photo/AP
Karak is home to a minority Christian population. In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff. Jordan's Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition. King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan "will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties" and offered his "deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded."
Jordan's Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism. Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman. Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world's foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday's shooting, calling it a "heinous terrorist attack." Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and "affirmed Iraq's solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism," Hussein's office said in a statement. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as "especially heinous," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. "The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account."
